notes.meaning: Asaph cries out to God with his whole voice in a time of great distress. He repeats his cry to show how urgent and earnest his prayer is. He remains confident that God hears him, even while the trouble is still heavy.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church teaching notes that many people only cry to God for earthly gifts like health or money, but true prayer seeks God Himself.

notes.meaning: In his darkest hours, the writer turns straight to the Lord instead of seeking earthly distractions. He reaches out his hands in prayer all night without giving up. Yet his pain is so sharp that ordinary words of comfort cannot bring him peace.

When he remembers God, the thought brings him sorrow instead of comfort because he feels God is angry with him. He meditates on his painful condition until his strength fades and his spirit faints. Even faithful believers can experience times when thinking about God feels overwhelming.
His grief is so severe that it feels as if God is holding his eyelids open, keeping him from sleep. The sorrow stuns and exhausts his mind. He is so shaken that he cannot even find words to speak.

To find some relief, the writer turns his thoughts back to ancient times and past generations. He looks to the history of God's people to see how the Lord treated them in their trials. Remembering God's long record of help gives troubled hearts a place to rest.

During the quiet hours of the night, he recalls the songs of thanks he used to sing in happier seasons. He searches his heart deeply, asking why these troubles have fallen upon him. He examines his soul to understand what God is doing in his life.

The writer pours out the anxious questions that weigh down his heart. He asks whether the Lord has rejected His people for good, whether His loyal love is gone, and whether His promises have failed forever. He wonders if God's anger has locked away His tender mercy. Speaking these hard questions aloud helps him confront his fears honestly before God.

The writer stops himself and recognizes that these fearful thoughts spring from the weakness of his own faith. He grieves over the feeling that God's strong right hand of protection has changed toward him. Acknowledging his human weakness marks the moment he begins turning away from despair.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Several scholars read the line as the Berean Standard Bible (BSB) translation in these notes does. On this reading his real grief is that God's right hand seems to have changed. He is stating his sorrow plainly, not correcting himself yet.

notes.meaning: To steady his soul, the writer chooses to focus on the great miracles God performed in the past. He spends time quietly thinking through the Lord's mighty acts of rescue. He also speaks of these works to others, finding that declaring God's deeds strengthens his own faith.

God's ways are holy, righteous, and completely pure. Even when His providential plans seem mysterious to human eyes, worshiping in His presence shows that He does all things well. No false idol or earthly power can ever compare to the greatness of our God.

The Lord is the only true God who performs wonders beyond all human ability. He did not hide His mighty power, but showed it openly before the nations of the world. What He did for His people proved His supremacy over every earthly ruler.

With great strength, God redeemed His people by freeing them from hard bondage in Egypt. Joseph is named along with Jacob to honor how Joseph cared for the family during the famine and trusted in God's future rescue. This ancient rescue serves as a lasting reminder that God delivers those who belong to Him.

The waters of the Red Sea are pictured as if they were living things that saw their Creator and trembled in awe. When God drew near, the deep sea parted before His almighty command. Even nature obeys the voice of its Maker without hesitation.

A tremendous storm broke out as God delivered Israel, with pouring rain, booming thunder, and flashes of lightning darting like arrows across the sky. The whirlwind roared and an earthquake shook the ground beneath the Egyptians. God used the full force of the skies and the earth to protect His people and defeat their enemies.

God carved a path right through the deep waters of the sea to bring His people across safely. His divine power was clearly at work, yet His actual footprints could not be seen once the waters returned to their place. God often works in unseen, mysterious ways that human eyes cannot track.

God guided the people of Israel with the gentleness of a shepherd caring for a flock of sheep. He chose Moses and Aaron as His servants to guide, protect, and direct them through the dry wilderness. The same mighty God who controls the stormy seas cares tenderly for each of His people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Because the psalm stops so abruptly, some scholars think part of it was lost or that it was never finished. Others reply that the Asaph psalms often end on a scene from history like this one.
